title: Tiramisù
subtitle: coffee and mascarpone cream dessert
excerpt: Tiramisù layers coffee-soaked savoiardi biscuits with a rich mascarpone cream made from egg yolks whisked with sugar and marsala wine. It needs at least four hours in the fridge to set, and the flavour deepens further overnight. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Tiramisù was created in the Veneto region of northern Italy, most likely in the 1960s or 1970s. The name means 'pick me up' in Italian, a reference to the coffee and the uplifting richness of the cream. It spread quickly across Italy and became one of the country's most internationally recognised desserts.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before. Chill overnight for the best texture.

glossaryTerms.definition: An Italian dessert meaning 'pick me up', made with layers of coffee-soaked sponge and mascarpone cream.
A rich Italian cream cheese made from double cream, with a mild, slightly sweet flavour.

content.text: is a no-bake Italian dessert built in layers: coffee-soaked biscuits at the base, followed by a cloud of

cream, then more biscuits, then more cream, finished with a dusting of cocoa. The technique is whisking the egg yolks and sugar until pale and thick before folding in the mascarpone, which gives the cream its lightness. This recipe serves 4.
The dessert needs time in the fridge to set properly. Four hours is the minimum, but overnight is better. The biscuits soften from crisp to the texture of sponge cake as they absorb the coffee.
Dissolve the espresso powder in 200ml of hot water. Stir in the amaretto. Pour into a shallow bowl and leave to cool.
Whisk the egg yolks and caster sugar together in a large bowl until the mixture is pale, thick and leaves a ribbon when you lift the whisk, about 4 to 5 minutes.

Add the marsala wine to the egg mixture and whisk briefly to combine. Add the mascarpone and fold gently with a spatula until smooth and well combined. Do not overwork or the cream will become too loose.
Dip savoiardi biscuits one at a time into the cooled coffee, letting each one soak for about 2 seconds per side. They should be moist through but not falling apart.
Arrange a single layer of soaked biscuits in the base of a rectangular dish. Spread half the mascarpone cream evenly over the top.
Add a second layer of soaked biscuits, then spread the remaining cream over the top. Smooth the surface with a palette knife or the back of a spoon.
Cover with cling film and refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight. Before serving, dust the top generously with cocoa powder through a fine sieve.

attrs.symptom: Cream is runny and will not hold its shape
attrs.cause: Mascarpone was overmixed or the egg yolks were not whisked thick enough
attrs.fix: Whisk yolks and sugar until genuinely ribbon-stage thick before adding mascarpone, then fold rather than whisk once they are combined

attrs.symptom: Biscuits are soggy and have dissolved into the cream
attrs.cause: They were soaked too long in the coffee mixture
attrs.fix: Dip each biscuit for no more than 2 seconds per side; they will continue to soften in the fridge

attrs.symptom: Dessert has not set after 4 hours
attrs.cause: The cream was too loose when assembled or the fridge is not cold enough
attrs.fix: Leave overnight; if the texture is still very soft, the egg yolks needed longer whisking at the start

content.text: Tiramisù appears on every Italian restaurant menu in the world. In the Veneto region, where it was first made, it is treated with some seriousness. The biscuits used are always savoiardi, known elsewhere as ladyfingers or sponge fingers. Coffee quality matters. Use proper espresso powder or a very strong brew rather than instant granules.
